A p-type semiconductor is made by doping tetravalent Si or Ge with a TRIVALENT impurity (B, Al, In), which carries one valence electron fewer than the host atom. Each such acceptor atom can bond with only three of its four Si neighbours, so it leaves one bond vacant, i.e. it contributes one hole. These doped holes far outnumber the thermally generated electron-hole pairs, while the only source of conduction electrons is that weak intrinsic generation, and the extra holes also speed up recombination of those electrons.
Hence for a p-type semiconductor \(n_h \gg n_e\): holes are the majority carriers and electrons are the minority carriers, and the dopant is trivalent.
So the statement of Exercise 14.1 that is true for a p-type semiconductor is: holes are majority carriers and trivalent atoms are the dopants.

The output frequency of a rectifier is the rate at which output pulses appear across the load.
Half-wave rectifier: the diode is forward biased for only one half of each input cycle, so the load carries ONE pulse per input cycle. The output therefore repeats at the input frequency, \(f_{\text{out}} = f_{\text{in}} = 50\,\text{Hz}\).
Full-wave rectifier: the two diodes conduct on alternate half-cycles, so a pulse appears across the load in EVERY half cycle, i.e. two pulses per input cycle. The output therefore repeats at twice the input frequency, \(f_{\text{out}} = 2 f_{\text{in}} = 2 \times 50\,\text{Hz} = 100\,\text{Hz}\).
Half-wave output frequency \(= 50\,\text{Hz}\); full-wave output frequency \(= 100\,\text{Hz}\).
